lessonTitle: Casting Basics: Sand and Die Casting, Shrinkage, Gates and Risers

blocks.text: A foundry pours a 400 mm aluminium pump cover from a pattern cut exactly to the drawing size. After cooling, the casting measures about 395 mm and the machinist has nothing left to cut. The metal shrank as it solidified and cooled, and nobody told the pattern maker.

blocks.markdown: Casting makes a part by pouring molten metal into a cavity and letting it solidify. The cavity is made from a **pattern**, a replica of the part, which is pressed into moulding sand (or used to shape a die). The two big families are **sand casting**, with a one-use mould, and **die casting**, with a permanent metal mould.

blocks.title: Pattern, mould, gate and riser
blocks.text: The **pattern** is a model of the part, slightly oversize, used to form the mould cavity. The **mould** is the cavity that receives the metal. The **gating system** (pouring basin, sprue, runner, gate) delivers metal into the cavity. A **riser** is an extra reservoir of molten metal attached to the casting that feeds it as it shrinks.

rows: Bonded sand, destroyed after each pour
Permanent steel die, used for many thousands of shots
Almost any alloy, including iron and steel
Mainly low-melting alloys: aluminium, zinc, magnesium
Usually small to medium, up to a few kilograms
Smooth, tight tolerance, thin walls possible
blocks.caption: Typical comparison; exact values depend on alloy and part.

blocks.markdown: In **die casting** the molten metal is forced into a steel die under pressure, solidifies in seconds and the die opens to eject the part. The expensive die pays back only if many parts are made, so die casting suits high-volume, thin-walled, accurate parts such as gearbox covers and phone chassis. Sand casting suits large, heavy or low-volume parts such as machine beds, pump casings and engine blocks, and is the only practical route for large iron or steel castings.

**Shrinkage allowance.** Metal contracts as it cools from the solidification temperature to room temperature. To get a casting of the correct final size the pattern must be made larger. If the linear shrinkage is $s$ (a fraction), the pattern dimension is found from the casting dimension. Typical values are about 1 % for grey cast iron, about 1.3 % for aluminium alloys and about 2 % for steel, but they depend on the alloy and part shape.

blocks.caption: Pattern dimension for a required casting dimension, linear shrinkage fraction s, ignoring machining allowance.

blocks.title: Pattern size for an aluminium plate
blocks.prompt: A cast aluminium plate must be 250 mm long. Using $s=1.3\,\%$ (typical), what is the pattern length?

steps.text: Write the shrinkage as a fraction: $s=0.013$.
Apply the pattern formula to the required length.
Evaluate: 250 x 1.013 = 253.25 mm. The pattern is 3.25 mm longer than the part.

blocks.title: Machining allowance and shrinkage together
blocks.prompt: A cast steel housing needs a finished length of 420 mm after machining. The casting is machined on both end faces, with 3 mm machining allowance on each. Using $s=2.0\,\%$, find the pattern length.

steps.text: The casting before machining must be longer than the finished part by the allowance on both faces: 420 + 3 + 3 = 426 mm.
Shrinkage acts on the whole casting, so scale this length by $(1+s)$.

blocks.answer: The pattern length is 434.52 mm. Applying shrinkage to the finished length only (428.4 mm) would leave the casting too short after machining.

blocks.markdown: **Gating system.** Metal is poured into a basin, flows down the vertical **sprue**, along the **runner** and enters the cavity through one or more **gates**. The gating system is designed to fill the cavity smoothly and quickly, without turbulence that would draw in air or break up oxide films, to trap slag and dirt (a runner well or filter), and to deliver metal to the cavity so that hot metal reaches the thick sections.

**Risers.** As metal solidifies it shrinks in volume (liquid contraction and solidification contraction). Without extra metal, the last region to freeze develops a shrinkage cavity. A riser is placed on the thick section of the casting and must stay liquid longer than the casting so that it can feed it. Chvorinov's rule gives the solidification time from the **modulus** $V/A$, the volume divided by the cooling surface area.

blocks.caption: Chvorinov's rule: solidification time ts, mould constant B (depends on mould material and metal), volume V and cooling surface area A of the shape.

blocks.title: Sizing a riser by modulus
blocks.prompt: A rectangular casting block 100 mm x 100 mm x 50 mm needs a riser whose modulus is at least 1.2 times the casting modulus (a typical design rule). Find the casting modulus and the minimum riser modulus.

steps.text: Volume: 100 x 100 x 50 = 500 000 mm^3. Cooling area: two faces of 100 x 100 plus four sides, two of 100 x 50 and two of 100 x 50.
Riser modulus must exceed this by the 1.2 factor so the riser freezes last: 1.2 x 12.5 = 15 mm.

blocks.answer: The casting modulus is 12.5 mm and the riser modulus must be at least 15 mm. Because $t_s\propto M^2$, the riser then freezes about 1.44 times later.

blocks.title: A riser that freezes first is useless
blocks.text: If a riser solidifies before the casting, it cannot feed the shrinking metal and the shrinkage cavity forms in the casting. Risers go on the heaviest sections, and the casting must freeze progressively toward the riser.

points: Sand casting uses an expendable sand mould with a low-cost pattern and suits large or low-volume parts and high-melting alloys; die casting uses a permanent steel die and suits high-volume, thin-walled, accurate non-ferrous parts.
Pattern dimensions are the casting dimensions multiplied by (1 + s), applied to the size including any machining allowance.

Gates and runners deliver metal smoothly and trap dirt; risers hold liquid metal that feeds shrinkage and must solidify after the casting, which Chvorinov's rule (time proportional to modulus squared) is used to check.

questions.stem: A company will make 250 000 thin-walled aluminium electronics housings with smooth surfaces and tight tolerances. Which process is most suitable?

options.text: High-pressure die casting
Sand casting with a wooden pattern
Hand-moulded loam casting
Forging from a hot billet

distractorRationale.b: Sand casting gives rough surfaces and wide tolerances, and a hand-moulded pattern is uneconomical at this volume.
distractorRationale.c: Loam moulding is a slow method for very large one-off castings.
distractorRationale.d: Forging does not give thin-walled hollow housings of this shape.

questions.explanation: Die casting uses a hardened steel die that can produce hundreds of thousands of accurate parts, so the high tooling cost is spread thinly. Sand casting is better for low volumes and large parts.

questions.stem: A 2.5 tonne grey iron machine bed is needed, with only three units required. Which process is the best fit?

options.text: Sand casting
High-pressure die casting
Cold-chamber die casting in aluminium
Injection moulding

distractorRationale.b: Die casting dies for a 2.5 tonne iron part would be impractically large and costly, and iron is not die cast.
distractorRationale.c: Aluminium does not have the stiffness and damping needed and this is not die cast at this size.

questions.explanation: Sand casting handles very large parts and iron and steel alloys, and the pattern is cheap compared with a die. For three units, the high tooling cost of die casting could never be recovered.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a riser on a sand casting?

options.text: To act as a reservoir of liquid metal that feeds the casting while it shrinks during solidification
To let air escape so that the sand mould does not crack
To reduce the speed of metal entering the cavity
To make the pattern easier to withdraw from the sand

questions.correctOptionText: To act as a reservoir of liquid metal that feeds the casting while it shrinks during solidification

distractorRationale.b: Vents release air and gas; a riser is a metal reservoir.
distractorRationale.c: Slowing the metal is a function of the gating system, such as the sprue and runner design.
distractorRationale.d: Draft angles on the pattern make withdrawal easier.

questions.explanation: A riser stays molten longer than the casting and supplies liquid to make up for the volume lost as the casting solidifies. Without it, a shrinkage cavity forms in the last section to freeze.

questions.stem: Why is the gating system of a sand mould designed to fill the cavity with low turbulence?

options.text: Turbulent flow entrains air and breaks oxide films, creating porosity and inclusions
Turbulence cools the metal too quickly and makes it set in the sprue
Turbulent metal erodes the pattern
Low turbulence is needed so the metal shrinks less

questions.correctOptionText: Turbulent flow entrains air and breaks oxide films, creating porosity and inclusions

distractorRationale.b: Cooling is determined by heat transfer, not mainly by turbulence in the sprue.
distractorRationale.c: The pattern has been removed before pouring, so it cannot be eroded.
distractorRationale.d: Shrinkage depends on the alloy and cooling, not on filling turbulence.

questions.explanation: Rapid, turbulent flow folds air and oxide skin into the metal, leaving gas porosity and oxide inclusions that weaken the casting. Smooth filling through a well-designed sprue, runner and gate reduces these defects.

questions.stem: A designer needs a casting of exact final size. Which statement about the pattern is correct?

options.text: The pattern is larger than the final casting by the shrinkage allowance
The pattern is smaller than the casting because the sand expands
The pattern equals the casting size because the mould is flexible
The pattern is smaller, because the metal expands as it solidifies

questions.correctOptionText: The pattern is larger than the final casting by the shrinkage allowance

distractorRationale.b: Sand does not make the casting expand; the metal contracts.
distractorRationale.c: The mould cannot make up for the contraction of cooling metal.
distractorRationale.d: Metals contract overall from solidification to room temperature, so the pattern must be oversize.

questions.explanation: As the casting cools it contracts, so the cavity, and hence the pattern, must be larger than the finished part by the shrinkage allowance. Making the pattern the same size gives an undersize casting.

questions.stem: A brass casting must be 380 mm long. Take the linear shrinkage for the alloy as 1.3 % (assumed). What pattern length, in mm, is needed? Ignore machining allowance.
questions.explanation: The pattern length is $380\times(1+0.013)=384.94$ mm. The pattern is therefore 4.94 mm longer than the finished part to allow for contraction on cooling.

questions.stem: A pattern for an aluminium casting measures 512.6 mm. The alloy has linear shrinkage of 1.3 %. What is the length of the casting at room temperature, in mm?
questions.explanation: Since $L_{pattern}=L_{casting}(1+s)$, the casting length is $512.6/1.013=506.02$ mm. The casting is shorter than the pattern because it contracts on cooling.

questions.stem: A spherical casting has a diameter of 8 cm. Chvorinov's mould constant is $B=3$ min/cm$^2$. Using modulus $V/A$ with $V=\pi D^3/6$ and $A=\pi D^2$, find the solidification time in minutes.
questions.explanation: The modulus of a sphere is $D/6=1.333$ cm. The time is $t=3\times(1.333)^2=5.33$ min. A riser attached to this casting would need a longer solidification time.

questions.stem: Explain the functions of the gating system and of a riser in a sand casting, and state why the riser must solidify after the casting.
markingGuide: Gating system delivers metal to the cavity (sprue, runner, gate) with low turbulence
Traps slag and dirt and avoids air entrainment
Riser is a reservoir of liquid metal to feed volume contraction during solidification
Riser attached to heavy section and prevents shrinkage cavity in casting
Riser must freeze last so that it can still supply liquid; modulus larger than casting (Chvorinov, time proportional to modulus squared)
questions.explanation: A good answer separates the two roles: gates fill the cavity smoothly, risers compensate for shrinkage. The riser must remain liquid while the casting freezes, otherwise a cavity forms in the casting.

questions.stem: Compare sand casting and die casting for (a) a 40 kg pump casing in cast iron, 30 off, and (b) a zinc connector body, 500 000 off. Justify the choice for each.
markingGuide: (a) sand casting: iron is a high-melting alloy not suited to ordinary die casting
(a) low volume and large size make permanent die tooling uneconomic
(b) die casting: high volume spreads the high die cost
(b) zinc is a low-melting alloy suited to die casting with good finish and tolerance
Mentions surface finish and tolerance or tooling cost trade-off
questions.explanation: The choice follows from alloy, size and volume: sand for large, low-volume, high-melting parts; die casting for small, high-volume, low-melting parts needing accuracy. The tooling cost versus volume trade-off is the central argument.
